blocks.text: Quick verdict

Webshare is the better choice for developers and scraping on a budget: $27.50 for 10 GB against $45 at NodeMaven's pay-as-you-go rate, a larger advertised pool and a free datacenter tier for testing. NodeMaven is the better choice for social media and multi-account work, where pre-screened IPs, mobile proxies (Webshare has none), sticky sessions longer than Webshare's 24 hours and rollover traffic matter, and at 100 GB its $2.20/GB monthly rate is slightly cheaper than Webshare's $2.25.

NodeMaven and Webshare both offer self-service residential and static ISP proxies with SOCKS5, but they target different buyers. Webshare is a developer favourite with low monthly prices, an 80M+ advertised pool and a free datacenter plan. NodeMaven targets account operators with IP quality filtering, mobile IPs on the same balance, long sticky sessions and rollover. This comparison shows which one fits scraping and which fits account management.

blocks.text: NodeMaven in 2026: what you get

NodeMaven is the quality-first option. Instead of handing out whatever IP the pool returns, it screens addresses in real time and lets you choose how strict the screening is. That matters most for account-based work such as social media management and multi-accounting, where a flagged IP can cost you an account. The price reflects it: $4.50/GB without a plan and $2.20/GB on monthly plans.

Strengths: IP Quality Filter screens IPs before you get them; Long sticky sessions for account work; Traffic rollover and cashback; Quality guarantee that pays for bad IPs. Weak spots: Smaller pool than mass-market networks; No datacenter proxies; Pay-as-you-go rate is double the plan rate.
Webshare in 2026: what you get

Webshare is the self-service favourite of solo developers. It gives away 10 shared datacenter proxies with 1 GB a month forever, sells paid datacenter lists from $2.99 for 100 proxies, and offers static ISP and rotating residential networks with a clean dashboard and good API. Its rotating residential pool is listed at 80M+ IPs in 195 countries, with sticky sessions from one minute to 24 hours. The main catch is that monthly bandwidth resets every 30 days and does not roll over.

Strengths: Permanent free datacenter plan for testing; Low, transparent residential pricing; Excellent dashboard and API; Sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Weak spots: Bandwidth resets monthly with no rollover; No mobile proxies; 500-request default concurrency limit.
Pricing: NodeMaven vs Webshare

NodeMaven charges $4.50/GB pay-as-you-go and $2.20/GB on monthly plans, with residential and mobile traffic on one balance. A $3.50 trial includes 750 MB. Unused traffic rolls over, and you earn up to 10% cashback on used traffic. ISP proxies start at $2.99 per IP with unlimited traffic.

Webshare's rotating residential plans cost $3.50 for 1 GB, $27.50 for 10 GB, $65 for 25 GB, $225 for 100 GB and $875 for 500 GB per month, falling to $1.40/GB at 3 TB. Yearly billing is about 30% cheaper but is paid upfront for a 360-day term. Unused bandwidth resets every 30 days.

For a 10 GB month, Webshare costs about $27.50 while NodeMaven costs about $45, so Webshare saves around 39%. For 100 GB, there is little to separate them on price ($220 for NodeMaven, $225 for Webshare). The sticker price is only half of it. NodeMaven's unused traffic carries forward, while Webshare's does not (allowance resets every 30 days; no rollover), so if your usage swings from month to month NodeMaven can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, Webshare (80M+) is about 2.7x larger than NodeMaven (30M+ residential + 250K mobile). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, NodeMaven lists 150+ countries and Webshare lists 195. On targeting, NodeMaven offers country, region, city and ISP, while Webshare offers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, NodeMaven offers rotating or long sticky sessions (multi-day), and Webshare offers rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: Webshare. Webshare has the edge here. Why: low prices and a developer-friendly API. How NodeMaven compares: the quality filter matters less for high-rotation crawling.

SERP and rank tracking: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With NodeMaven: workable, but you pay a premium for filtering you may not need. With Webshare: fine for light rank tracking. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Social media and multi-account management: NodeMaven wins. The deciding factor for NodeMaven: pre-screened, low-fraud-score IPs with long sticky sessions. The limitation on the Webshare side: 24-hour sticky sessions and cheap static ISP IPs.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With NodeMaven: fine for light checks. With Webshare: good for US work with ZIP targeting, thinner elsewhere. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Ad verification and geo-testing: NodeMaven. NodeMaven has the edge here. Why: good quality but a smaller pool. How Webshare compares: no mobile network and limited selector combinations.
Tight budgets: Webshare. Webshare has the edge here. Why: free tier plus some of the lowest per-GB rates here. How NodeMaven compares: mid-priced on plans, expensive on PAYG.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB. Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. Verification and payment rules differ too. NodeMaven: Standard. Webshare: ID checks only when flagged or for restricted categories. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test NodeMaven and Webshare before you commit
The quickest way to choose between NodeMaven and Webshare is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB; Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, NodeMaven comes out ahead in 2, Webshare in 2, and 2 are ties. With no overall winner, decide on the factor that matters most to you: NodeMaven is strongest for social media and multi-account management, while Webshare is strongest for solo developers and small teams. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
